title: Fine-Tuning

techniques.name: Prompt vs RAG vs Fine-Tune
techniques.q: Should I change the prompt, the context or the weights?
techniques.what: Most problems are solved without touching weights. Change the prompt when instructions or examples are missing; add retrieval when the model needs facts, especially facts that change; fine-tune when you need consistent behaviour, format, style or a narrow skill at high volume, and have good examples. Fine-tuning teaches behaviour better than knowledge: tuning on new facts can even raise hallucination.

When a vendor proposes training a model on your documents
When prompt and RAG results have plateaued on evals

Fine-tune only with enough good examples, enough volume and an owner for upkeep
pitfalls: Fine-tuning to “teach” facts that change monthly
Skipping a strong prompt baseline, so gains are overstated

tools: Amazon Bedrock and Vertex AI tuning
techniques.remember: Prompt for instructions, retrieve for facts, tune for behaviour.
techniques.cap: Illustrative rules; measure your own baseline first.

techniques.name: Supervised Fine-Tuning with LoRA and QLoRA
techniques.q: How do I teach a model a skill or format cheaply?
techniques.what: Supervised fine-tuning trains a model on input–output examples of the behaviour you want. LoRA freezes the original weights and trains small low-rank matrices beside them, cutting trainable parameters by orders of magnitude; QLoRA also stores the frozen weights in 4 bits, so large models fit on a single GPU. The adapter is a small file you can swap per task.

A narrow task with a few thousand good examples
Shrinking long prompts into the weights at high volume

around 1e-4 for adapters versus about 2e-5 for full fine-tuning

techniques.name: Preference Tuning with DPO
techniques.q: How do I teach a model which answer is better?
techniques.what: Direct Preference Optimization trains on pairs: for each prompt, a chosen and a rejected answer. It raises the likelihood of chosen answers relative to rejected ones while a parameter, beta, keeps the model close to a reference, without training a separate reward model as RLHF does. It usually follows SFT, and it learns whatever the pairs share, including biases such as longer answers always being chosen.

Fixing a known failure with pairs of good and bad responses

pitfalls: Noisy or inconsistent preferences, so the signal cancels out

techniques.remember: Clean pairs, moderate beta, watch length and regressions.

techniques.name: Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards
techniques.q: Can I train on answers a program can check?
techniques.what: When correctness can be checked by a program, such as unit tests, an exact numeric answer or a schema, the model can learn by trial: sample several answers per prompt, score each with the checker, and update towards the better ones. GRPO does this by comparing each answer with its group’s average, without a value model. It powered reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1. The checker must be hard to game, or the model learns to exploit it.
use: Maths, code, SQL and structured extraction with a checkable answer
Improving reasoning on tasks with a clear right answer
When SFT data is scarce but a verifier is cheap
metrics: a program returns a score: tests pass, answer matches, schema valid

pitfalls: Rewarding format alone, so the model learns the format and not the task

techniques.remember: Reward what a program can check, and check the checker.

techniques.name: Distillation into a Small Model
techniques.q: Can a small model learn to do what the big one does?
techniques.what: Distillation uses a large teacher model’s outputs on your real inputs as training data for a small student. Filter the teacher’s answers with a judge or verifier, optionally include its reasoning, and fine-tune the student, often with LoRA. Then route most traffic to the student and keep the teacher as a fallback. It is the usual way to turn an expensive frontier-model workload into an affordable one.

Cost or latency limits that rule out a large model on every call
Data that must stay on your own infrastructure

techniques.name: Evaluate Before and After Tuning
techniques.q: Did tuning actually make it better, and what did it break?
techniques.what: A tuned model must beat a strong prompted baseline on a held-out test set that never appeared in training, by more than the noise, and must not lose general skills or safety behaviour along the way. Deduplicate test items against training data, size the test set for the difference you expect, and run general and safety suites, because fine-tuning can cause catastrophic forgetting.

techniques.name: Training Data Curation and Synthetic Data
techniques.q: Is my fine-tuning data clean, balanced and safe to train on?
techniques.what: Curation builds the fine-tuning dataset itself: source examples from logs and experts, put them in one label set and one format, remove exact and near duplicates, fix wrong labels, balance intents and languages, scrub personal data, drop anything that overlaps the eval set, and fill thin intents with synthetic examples from a stronger model that are checked before use. A small, clean, consistent set usually beats a large noisy one. The training methods live in SFT, DPO and distillation; proving the result lives in Before and after.

A task where a few intents dominate and rare ones matter most
Any dataset that may hold customers’ personal data

techniques.name: Fine-Tuning for Tool Use and Agent Trajectories
techniques.q: Can a small model learn to use our tools as well as a big one?
techniques.what: General supervised fine-tuning teaches style and format; agent fine-tuning teaches a model to act. Each example is a whole trajectory: the user request, the assistant’s tool calls with arguments, the tool results and the final reply, in the model’s own chat and tool-call template. Trajectories come from production logs or from a strong teacher model run in a sandbox, and only those verified to have succeeded are kept. Loss is computed on assistant turns only, so the model learns to call tools rather than to invent tool results. The payoff is a small model that runs your agent loop at a fraction of the cost and latency, judged on end-to-end task success, not on text similarity. LoRA mechanics are covered by Supervised Fine-Tuning; learning from rewards by RLVR.

Proprietary tools and schemas a general model keeps getting wrong
On-premise agents where a large hosted model is not allowed

def choose_approach(task, evals, volume_per_month, n_examples):
    bar = task.required_accuracy               # from a real eval set       #@1
    if evals["prompt"] >= bar:                                              #@2
        return "prompt"                        # cheapest, easiest to change #@2
    if task.needs_facts and evals["rag"] >= bar:                            #@3
        return "rag"                           # facts live in retrieval     #@3
    worth_tuning = volume_per_month >= 100_000 and n_examples >= 1_000      #@4
    if not worth_tuning:                                                    #@4
        return "rag" if task.needs_facts else "prompt + better examples"    #@4
    if task.needs_facts:                                                    #@5
        return "rag + fine-tuned model"        # tune behaviour, retrieve facts  #@5
    return "fine-tune"                         # format, style, narrow skill #@5

# Re-run this when the base model, prices or the task change              #@6
steps: Measure a baseline and set the bar
The insurer built 500 real questions with checked answers before choosing anything. Without that, every option “seems to work”.
Try the prompt first
A structured prompt with examples and structured outputs is the cheapest change and the easiest to undo. It answered 71% here.
Facts go in retrieval
Policy wordings change, and answers need citations. Retrieval over the current PDFs reached 93%; tuning on them reached 76% and went stale.
Tuning has to pay for itself
Training, evaluation, hosting and retraining are fixed costs. Below about 100,000 calls a month, or without a thousand good examples, they are rarely recovered.
Tune for behaviour, retrieve facts
When the gap is format, tone or a narrow skill, tuning helps. When both matter, a tuned model reads retrieved context.
Revisit the decision
A new base model can make a tuned one obsolete, and a price change can move the break-even. Re-run the comparison.

steps: Collect reviewed conversations
5,000 real support chats, each checked so the reply follows the four-part format. The model learns exactly what it is shown, errors included.
Hold out a test set
10% is set aside and never trained on. Only held-out scores say whether the model learned the format or memorised the examples.
Train on the replies only
assistant_only_loss computes the loss on the assistant’s turns, so the model learns to answer, not to imitate customers.
Add a LoRA adapter
The 8B weights stay frozen. Small rank-16 matrices beside every linear layer are trained: about 0.5% of the parameters.
Quantise the base (QLoRA)
Storing the frozen base in 4-bit NF4 cuts its memory about four times, so training fits on a single 24 GB GPU.
Two epochs, then evaluate
More passes over 5,000 examples start to overfit. Format compliance on the held-out set rose from 81% to 97%.

steps: Collect preference pairs
For each question, advisers saw two answers and chose the better one. Judging is quicker and more consistent than writing ideal answers.
Drop pairs people disagree on
Pairs where reviewers disagreed are close to coin flips. Every mislabelled pair cancels a correct one, so cleaning beats collecting more.
Start from an SFT model
DPO refines a model that already follows instructions. On a raw base model it has too much to learn from preferences alone.
Set beta
beta keeps the model near the frozen reference. Too small, and it drifts and loses general skills; too large, and it barely changes. 0.1 is a common start.
Balance answer lengths
If the chosen answer is usually the longer one, the model learns that length wins. The first run here did exactly that.
Report more than the win rate
Win rate against the old model rose from 50% to 64%. Answer length and a general regression suite show whether that came at a cost.

def correct(completions, answer, **kwargs):
    rewards = []
    for text, key in zip(completions, answer):
        m = re.search(r"\\boxed\{(-?[\d.]+)\}", text)                          #@2
        ok = m and abs(float(m.group(1)) - float(key)) < 1e-6               #@2
        rewards.append(1.0 if ok else 0.0)       # no credit for format    #@5
    return rewards

trainer = GRPOTrainer(
    model="sft-maths-1b",
    reward_funcs=correct,                                                   #@2
    args=GRPOConfig(output_dir="grpo-maths",
                    num_generations=8,          # the group size          #@3
                    learning_rate=1e-6, max_steps=600),                   #@4
    train_dataset=data)
trainer.train()

steps: Problems with checkable answers
Each school maths problem has a numeric key. No human needs to judge a solution; a program can.
A verifier as the reward
The reward function parses one boxed number and compares it with the key: 1 if right, 0 if not. It must be hard to fool.
Sample a group per prompt
GRPO samples eight answers per problem and compares them with each other: answers above the group average are reinforced, those below are discouraged.
Train for enough steps
Accuracy climbs over hundreds of steps. Each step costs eight generations per prompt, so the group size and the number of steps set the bill.
Never pay for format alone
An earlier reward gave credit for a neatly boxed answer. Reward rose to 95% while accuracy stayed at 42%: the model learned the format, not the maths.
Judge by held-out accuracy
Training reward can be gamed. Accuracy on held-out problems, checked independently, rose from 58% after SFT to 66%.

def build_dataset(logged, checker, keep_rationale=True):
    rows = []
    for r in logged:                            # teacher answers from logs  #@1
        if not checker(r["query"], r["answer"]):                            #@2
            continue                            # drop teacher mistakes      #@2
        target = (f"{r['rationale']}\nAnswer: {r['answer']}"                #@3
                  if keep_rationale else r["answer"])                        #@3
        rows.append({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": r["query"]},
                                  {"role": "assistant", "content": target}]})
    return rows

student = sft_train("base-8b", build_dataset(load_logged(), passes_checks))  #@4

def route(query, threshold=0.8):
    answer, confidence = student(query)                                     #@5
    return answer if confidence >= threshold else teacher(query)             #@5

def dedupe(test, train, threshold=0.8):
    lsh = MinHashLSH(threshold=threshold, num_perm=128)                     #@1
    for i, t in enumerate(train):                                           #@1
        lsh.insert(str(i), minhash(t["text"]))                              #@1
    return [t for t in test if not lsh.query(minhash(t["text"]))]           #@1

def gain_with_ci(base_scores, tuned_scores):
    diffs = [t - b for b, t in zip(base_scores, tuned_scores)]              #@3
    n = len(diffs)
    mean = sum(diffs) / n
    sd = math.sqrt(sum((d - mean) ** 2 for d in diffs) / (n - 1))
    return mean, 1.96 * sd / math.sqrt(n)                                   #@3

clean = dedupe(load("test_1000.jsonl"), load("train.jsonl"))                #@2

Near-duplicates of training examples inflate scores. Here 30% of the original test set had them.
Use enough test cases
With 50 cases, the margin of error on a difference is about ±16 points. With 1,000 it is about ±3.5.
Report the gain with an interval
Scoring both models on the same cases and giving a confidence interval shows whether the gain is real.
Compare with the best baseline
Beating the untuned base is easy. The question is whether tuning beats the best prompted or RAG setup.
Check what tuning broke
General-knowledge and safety suites, run on both models with the same settings, show forgetting that the target task hides.

The real gain was 4 points, with drops of 6 on general questions and 3 on refusals. The tuned model now handles notes only.

from datasketch import MinHash, MinHashLSH
from cleanlab.filter import find_label_issues

rows = load_logs("loan_queries.jsonl") + load_expert_examples()   # 50,000  #@1
rows = [normalise(r) for r in rows]      # one intent set, one chat format    #@1

def sig(text, n=5):
    m = MinHash(num_perm=128)
    for i in range(max(1, len(text) - n + 1)):
        m.update(text[i:i + n].encode("utf-8"))
    return m

lsh, seen, kept = MinHashLSH(threshold=0.8, num_perm=128), set(), []      #@2
for i, r in enumerate(rows):
    text = r["text"].lower()
    h, m = hashlib.sha256(text.encode()).hexdigest(), sig(text)             #@2
    if h in seen or lsh.query(m):
        continue                         # exact or near copy: 9,000 dropped  #@2
    seen.add(h); lsh.insert(str(i), m); kept.append((r, m))

evl = MinHashLSH(threshold=0.8, num_perm=128)                              #@3
for j, e in enumerate(load_eval("eval_2000.jsonl")):                       #@3

steps: Source and normalise

Udaan Lend, a fictional NBFC, pulls 50,000 loan queries from 14 months of chat and call-centre logs, plus a few hundred replies written by collections and grievance experts. normalise() maps old label spellings onto one set of 12 intents and puts every row in the same chat format, so the model never sees “EMI date” and “emi_due_date” as two different answers.
Remove exact and near duplicates

A SHA-256 hash catches exact copies. MinHash signatures on 5-character shingles, indexed with LSH, catch near-copies at Jaccard similarity 0.8, such as the same template with a different name. 9,000 rows, 18%, go. Copies over-weight a few phrasings and waste review effort.
Decontaminate against the eval set

The same signatures are checked against the 2,000-item eval set. 400 training rows are near-copies of eval items. Left in, the model memorises them: on the raw data the full eval set reports 84.9% while its 1,600 clean items show 81.4%. Removing them leaves 40,600 rows.
Find and fix wrong labels

find_label_issues compares each logged intent with cross-validated predictions and ranks the likely errors. The 2,000 hardest go to trained reviewers at ₹40 each, ₹80,000 in all; clear-cut ones are relabelled by a stronger model. Wrong labels fall from 9% to about 1.5%.
Scrub PII, then rebalance

12% of rows carry Aadhaar or PAN numbers, mobile numbers, names or loan account numbers. A model can repeat what it was trained on, and India’s DPDP Act expects personal data to be used only for a stated purpose, so scrub_pii() swaps them for typed placeholders such as [PAN], catching 98%. Then the EMI-due-date intent, 30% of rows, is cut to one in three: 8,120 rows go and 32,480 remain.
Add verified synthetic rows

Three rare intents, foreclosure quotes, restructuring requests and grievance escalation, have about 1,200 real rows. A stronger model writes 8,000 more in English, Hindi and Hinglish; checks keep 5,000 where an independent classifier agrees, facts match the policy sheet and nothing copies a real or eval row, and reviewers spot-check 500 for ₹20,000. Rare-intent accuracy rises from 58% to 87%, and overall to 90.6% on 37,480 rows.

steps: Store trajectories as chat messages
Yatra Setu, a fictional travel-booking company, logs each booking run as messages with tool calls and tool results, plus the tool schemas, in the same template the model will be served with.
Keep verified successes
A sandbox checks each run’s end state: was the right train held for the right date and seats? 2,000 of 3,100 teacher trajectories pass and are kept.
Mask everything but the assistant
With assistant-only loss, the model learns to write tool calls and replies. It never learns to write tool outputs, which is how models start inventing results.
Train a LoRA adapter
Two epochs of LoRA on an 8B model take a few GPU-hours. Data generation by the teacher was the larger cost.
Evaluate in the sandbox
300 held-out tasks run end to end. Score task success, valid tool calls and invented tool results, not text overlap.
Compare with the teacher
The base 8B model succeeds on 48% and the teacher on 78%; the tuned 8B reaches 73% at about one fifteenth of the cost per task.

import re
from datasets import load_dataset
from trl import GRPOConfig, GRPOTrainer

data = load_dataset("json", data_files="maths.jsonl")["train"]  # prompt, answer

def correct(completions, answer, **kwargs):
    """1.0 if the final boxed number matches the key, else 0.0."""
    rewards = []
    for text, key in zip(completions, answer):
        m = re.search(r"\\boxed\{(-?[\d.]+)\}", text)
        rewards.append(1.0 if m and abs(float(m.group(1)) - float(key)) < 1e-6 else 0.0)
    return rewards

trainer = GRPOTrainer(
    model="sft-maths-1b",
    reward_funcs=correct,
    args=GRPOConfig(output_dir="grpo-maths", num_generations=8,
                    learning_rate=1e-6, max_steps=600),
    train_dataset=data)
trainer.train()

import math
from datasketch import MinHash, MinHashLSH

def dedupe(test, train, threshold=0.8):
    """Drop test cases that have a near-duplicate in the training data."""
    lsh = MinHashLSH(threshold=threshold, num_perm=128)
    for i, t in enumerate(train):
        lsh.insert(str(i), minhash(t["text"]))
    return [t for t in test if not lsh.query(minhash(t["text"]))]

def gain_with_ci(base_scores, tuned_scores):
    """Difference in accuracy with a 95% confidence interval (paired items)."""
    diffs = [t - b for b, t in zip(base_scores, tuned_scores)]
    n = len(diffs)
    mean = sum(diffs) / n
    sd = math.sqrt(sum((d - mean) ** 2 for d in diffs) / (n - 1))
    return mean, 1.96 * sd / math.sqrt(n)

clean = dedupe(load("test.jsonl"), load("train.jsonl"))
for suite in [clean, load("general.jsonl"), load("safety.jsonl")]:

import hashlib
import re
from datasketch import MinHash, MinHashLSH

def sig(text, n=5, num_perm=128):
    """MinHash signature over character 5-grams of normalised text."""
    text = " ".join(text.lower().split())
    m = MinHash(num_perm=num_perm)
    for i in range(max(1, len(text) - n + 1)):
        m.update(text[i:i + n].encode("utf-8"))
    return m

def dedupe(rows, threshold=0.8):
    lsh, seen, kept = MinHashLSH(threshold=threshold, num_perm=128), set(), []
    for i, r in enumerate(rows):
        h = hashlib.sha256(" ".join(r["text"].lower().split()).encode()).hexdigest()
        m = sig(r["text"])
        if h in seen or lsh.query(m):
            continue                       # exact or near copy
        seen.add(h)
        lsh.insert(f"row-{i}", m)
        kept.append(r)
    return kept

def decontaminate(rows, eval_rows, threshold=0.8):
    lsh = MinHashLSH(threshold=threshold, num_perm=128)
    for j, e in enumerate(eval_rows):
        lsh.insert(f"eval-{j}", sig(e["text"]))
    return [r for r in rows if not lsh.query(sig(r["text"]))]

PII = [("AADHAAR", re.compile(r"\b\d{4}\s?\d{4}\s?\d{4}\b")),
       ("PAN", re.compile(r"\b[A-Z]{5}\d{4}[A-Z]\b")),
       ("MOBILE", re.compile(r"(?:\+91[\s-]?)?\b[6-9]\d{9}\b")),
       ("EMAIL", re.compile(r"\b[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.]+\b")),
       ("LOAN_AC", re.compile(r"\bUL\d{10}\b"))]

def scrub_pii(text):
    for tag, pattern in PII:
        text = pattern.sub(f"[{tag}]", text)
    return text

def cap_intent(rows, intent, keep_every=3):
    out, n = [], 0
    for r in rows:
        if r["intent"] == intent:
            n += 1
            if n % keep_every:
                continue                   # keep 1 in 3
        out.append(r)
    return out
datacur.note: scrub_pii() is a regex sketch; names and addresses need an NER-based tool such as Microsoft Presidio, plus a human check on a sample. The loan account format UL followed by 10 digits is invented for this example. Label-issue ranking uses cleanlab.filter.find_label_issues with cross-validated probabilities. decide.title: Building a fine-tuning dataset
decide.code:
def build_training_set(chats, help_pages):
    rows = [to_example(c) for c in chats]           # reviewed support chats
    rows += [qa_pairs_from(p) for p in help_pages]  # fee schedule, updated monthly
    return rows
decide.explain: Training on fee schedules bakes facts that change every month into the weights. The model goes stale after the next circular, cannot cite a source, and tuning on new facts can raise hallucination. Fees belong in retrieval.
decide.fix: # fees stay in retrieval over the current schedule; train on behaviour only

also.2: Correct: reviewed chats teach format and tone, which is what tuning is good at.

sft.code:
data = load_dataset("json", data_files="chats.jsonl")["train"]

dpo.title: Mapping adviser votes to DPO columns
dpo.code:
raw = load_dataset("json", data_files="adviser_votes.jsonl")["train"]
pairs = raw.map(lambda r: {"prompt": r["question"],
                           "chosen": r["answer_rejected_by_adviser"],
                           "rejected": r["answer_preferred_by_adviser"]})
dpo.explain: The columns are swapped: the answer advisers rejected is labelled chosen. DPO will faithfully push the model towards the answers people disliked.

also.2: Correct: the question becomes the prompt.

rlvr.title: The reward function
rlvr.explain: A substring check is easy to game: an answer listing many numbers, or “12” inside “120”, earns full reward. The model learns to hedge rather than solve. Parse one final answer and compare it exactly.
rlvr.fix: m = re.search(r"\\boxed\{(-?[\d.]+)\}", text); ok = bool(m) and float(m.group(1)) == float(key)

also.5: Correct: a binary reward for verified correctness.

distill.title: Routing between student and teacher
distill.explain: The comparison is inverted: the student answers when it is unsure and the teacher when the student is confident. Accuracy drops and the bill rises. Serve the student’s answer only when its confidence is at or above the threshold.
distill.fix: return answer if confidence >= threshold else teacher(query)

also.2: Correct: ask the student first; it is the cheap path.

tuneeval.title: Comparing base and tuned models
tuneeval.code:
train, test = split_by_customer(all_notes)
test = test + random.sample(train, 200)        # top up the test set
base_acc = score(BASE, test)
tuned_acc = score(TUNED, test)
print(f"gain: {tuned_acc - base_acc:+.1%}")
tuneeval.explain: Topping up the test set with training examples contaminates it: the tuned model has seen those cases, so the measured gain is inflated. Collect fresh cases instead, and report a confidence interval.
tuneeval.fix: test = test + collect_new_cases(200)          # never reuse training data

also.1: Correct: splitting by customer keeps related notes on one side.

datacur.title: Decontaminating against the eval set
datacur.explain: Eval signatures are built from the original text, but training signatures from lower-cased text. “EMI”, “PAN” and every capitalised word produce different shingles, so near-copies score below the 0.8 threshold and slip through: the eval set stays contaminated and the score stays inflated. Normalise both sides in exactly the same way.

also.2: Correct: the same threshold and num_perm must be used when querying.
also.8: Correct: a training row is kept only when no eval item is a near-copy of it.

ftagent.code:

cfg = SFTConfig(output_dir="booking-8b-lora", num_train_epochs=2,

ftagent.explain: Every teacher run is used, including the 35% that failed or looped. The model learns those failures as readily as the successes.
