decide.q: A colleague wants to fine-tune a model on your product documents. How do you respond?
decide.model: Ask what the gap is and measure first. If the model lacks facts, especially ones that change, retrieval over the documents is better: it updates instantly and cites sources, while fine-tuning adds new facts unreliably, goes stale and has been found to increase hallucination. Tune when the gap is behaviour, such as format or tone, and volume justifies it.

decide.q: When does fine-tuning pay for itself?
decide.model: When per-query savings, such as a shorter prompt or a smaller model, outweigh fixed costs for training, evaluation, hosting and retraining. That usually needs high volume, often above a hundred thousand queries a month, plus a thousand or more good examples and someone to own retraining when the base model changes.

decide.q: Can you combine RAG and fine-tuning? When would you?
decide.model: Yes. Retrieval supplies current facts and fine-tuning shapes behaviour: a model tuned to a house format, or to use retrieved passages and cite them well, reading fresh context at run time. Use it when both a knowledge gap and a behaviour gap exist and volume justifies tuning.

sft.q: Explain LoRA and QLoRA and why they matter.
sft.model: LoRA freezes the pretrained weights and trains small low-rank matrices beside them, cutting trainable parameters by orders of magnitude and memory by several times; the adapters are small files that can be swapped or merged. QLoRA also stores the frozen base in 4-bit NF4, so a 65–70B model can be tuned on one large GPU with quality close to 16-bit tuning.

sft.q: How would you prepare data for supervised fine-tuning?
sft.model: Collect real inputs with reviewed target outputs, since the model copies errors. Deduplicate, balance the cases you care about, and format them as chat messages. Hold out a test set before training and never train on it. Compute the loss on the assistant’s responses only, and start with a few thousand high-quality examples rather than many noisy ones.

sft.q: What goes wrong with too many epochs on a small dataset?
sft.model: The model memorises the training examples: training loss keeps falling while held-out performance stalls or drops, and outputs begin to copy training text. Watch held-out metrics every epoch, keep the best checkpoint, and prefer more data or fewer epochs.

dpo.q: Explain DPO and how it differs from RLHF with PPO.
pts: no reward model or RL loop
dpo.model: RLHF trains a reward model on human preferences and then optimises the policy against it with PPO. DPO skips both: it uses chosen and rejected pairs directly in a loss that raises the chosen answer’s likelihood relative to a frozen reference model, with beta controlling how far it may move. It is simpler, cheaper and more stable.

dpo.q: Your DPO model wins more comparisons but users complain it waffles. What happened, and how do you fix it?
dpo.model: The chosen answers were usually longer, so the model learned that length wins. Balance lengths in the pairs or add pairs where the shorter answer wins, consider length-controlled evaluation, and report average length alongside the win rate.

dpo.q: How do you get good preference data?
dpo.model: Use real prompts, generate two plausible answers, and have more than one trained reviewer compare them. Keep pairs where reviewers agree and drop coin-flip cases, since each mislabelled pair cancels a correct one. Audit a sample regularly for biases such as preferring length or confidence.

rlvr.q: What is RLVR, and when is it the right tool?
rlvr.model: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards trains a model with rewards computed by a program, such as matching a maths answer key or passing unit tests, instead of a learned reward model. It suits tasks with objective checks and has driven large gains in reasoning models; it does not suit open-ended writing without a reliable verifier.

For each prompt GRPO samples a group of answers, scores each with the reward, and uses each answer’s reward relative to the group mean, normalised by the group’s spread, as its advantage. Answers above the average are reinforced and those below discouraged, which removes the need for a separate value model as in PPO.

rlvr.q: Training reward keeps rising, but your model is not getting better. What do you do?
rlvr.model: Suspect reward hacking: the model has found a way to score without solving, such as format rewards or a loose matcher. Compare with accuracy on held-out problems checked independently, inspect high-reward samples, and tighten the verifier, for example by parsing one final answer and comparing it exactly.

distill.q: Explain distillation and why companies use it.
distill.model: A large teacher model answers many real queries; a smaller student is fine-tuned on those answers, often with the teacher’s reasoning. The student can come close to the teacher on the target task at a fraction of the cost and latency, and can run on-premises.

distill.q: How would you move traffic from a frontier model to a distilled one safely?
distill.model: First compare the student with the teacher on a large held-out set, including hard cases. Then route a small share of easy, common intents to it, keep the teacher as fallback for low-confidence or unusual queries, monitor quality, and increase the share gradually.

distill.q: What limits how good a distilled student can be?
distill.model: The student is bounded by the teacher’s quality, so filter out teacher mistakes; by its own capacity, so very small students plateau lower; and by how well the training data covers real traffic. Rationales help small students, but hard cases usually still need the teacher.

tuneeval.q: How do you prove a fine-tuned model is better?
tuneeval.model: Evaluate on a held-out set that was never used in training and has been deduplicated against it, large enough for the margin of error to be smaller than the effect. Score the tuned model and the best prompted or RAG baseline on the same cases, and report the difference with a confidence interval.

tuneeval.q: What can fine-tuning break, and how do you catch it?
tuneeval.model: Narrow tuning can cause forgetting of general knowledge and reasoning, weaker instruction following and fewer safety refusals. Catch it by running general and safety suites on both base and tuned models with identical settings, then decide whether to route by task or retune.

tuneeval.q: A team reports a 12-point gain on 50 test cases. What questions do you ask?
tuneeval.model: Was the test set contaminated: were any test cases, or near-copies, in the training data? With 50 cases the margin of error on a difference is about ±16 points, so is the gain even distinguishable from noise? What was the baseline: the untuned base or the best prompted setup? And what did the general and safety suites show?

datacur.q: How would you turn a year of support logs into a fine-tuning dataset?
datacur.model: Put everything into one label set and one chat format. Remove exact copies by hash and near-copies with MinHash, and drop anything that overlaps the eval set. Rank probable label errors with confident learning and have people review the hardest. Scrub Aadhaar, PAN, phone and account numbers and names, cap intents that dominate, and check languages are covered. Fill thin intents with verified synthetic rows, version the set, and measure on a clean held-out set.

datacur.q: A team says their tuned model scores 89.8% on the eval set. What would you check about the training data?
datacur.model: First, whether eval items or near-copies of them are in the training data: deduplicating within the training set alone does not catch that. Run MinHash between training rows and eval items, remove the overlaps and re-score. In the playground, deduplicating within training only reports 89.8% while clean items show 87.5%.

datacur.q: When would you use synthetic data, and how do you keep it from hurting the model?
datacur.model: Use it where real rows are scarce, such as rare intents, new products or languages, or where real data cannot be used. Generate with a stronger model, then keep only rows an independent classifier agrees with, whose facts match the policy, and that do not copy real or eval rows; have people spot-check a sample. Keep real data as the backbone, because training repeatedly on generated data narrows the model.

ftagent.q: How would you train a small model to replace a large one in your agent?
ftagent.model: Generate trajectories with the large model in a sandbox or take them from logs, keep verified successes, format them in the serving template, fine-tune with LoRA on assistant turns only, and compare end-to-end task success, valid calls and invented results with the teacher.

ftagent.q: ₹6 vs ₹0.40 a task, 50,000 tasks a month. Saving?
The tuned model sometimes replies with a booking PNR without calling hold_seat. Cause and fix?
ftagent.model: The model learned to write tool results because tool turns carried loss. Retrain with assistant-only loss and measure invented results in the sandbox; add a runtime check that a PNR comes from a real tool call.

cases.tag: Weights are the wrong place for facts
cases.title: The support bot a vendor wants to train on the fee schedule
cases.brief: A discount broker's support assistant runs on a frontier model and answers three million queries a month. The bill has reached ₹27 lakh. A vendor has pitched a fine-tuning project, and the CTO wants to know which techniques to apply and in what order to cut cost without hurting answers.
evidence: 80% of queries fall into about forty recurring intents: order status, margin, brokerage charges, account-opening steps.
Brokerage charges and exchange fees change most months after SEBI circulars and exchange notices, and answers have to match the schedule currently in force.
Two lakh logged answers from the frontier model are available, each rated correct or not by a support agent. They are raw logs, with duplicates, customer names and PAN numbers in them.
The vendor proposes fine-tuning a 70B open model on the fee schedules and help-centre pages so it “knows the business”, then switching all traffic to it at once.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.decide: Start here, because the vendor's proposal is wrong in a specific and expensive way. Fees change most months after SEBI circulars, and fine-tuning to teach facts that change monthly is the first pitfall of this whole module - every circular would mean a retrain, and between retrains the model would be confidently out of date. The fee schedule belongs in retrieval; what belongs in the weights is the skill of answering these forty intents in the house style. Establish a strong prompt-and-RAG baseline first, or any gain you measure later is overstated.
why.distill: This is the right shape for the cost problem: forty recurring intents covering 80% of three million queries a month is a narrow, high-volume task a frontier model already does well, which is exactly when a small model trained on its outputs pays. Do not switch all traffic at once - the vendor's plan names that pitfall for you - and run a head-to-head evaluation first.
why.datacur: Two lakh rated logs is a real asset and raw logs are not a dataset. Training on them as they are puts duplicates, wrong labels, customer names and PAN numbers straight into the weights, where no erasure request can reach them. Deduplicate across the training and eval sets rather than within training only, strip personal data, keep the agent ratings as labels, and rebalance so the rare intents that matter are not drowned by order-status queries.
why.tuneeval: The vendor's plan has no evaluation in it at all, which is how a project like this ships a regression. Measure the baseline before training, hold out a set large enough to separate a real gain from noise, keep test items out of the training data, and check the skills you did not target - a model tuned on forty intents can quietly lose the twentieth.
why.sft: Useful as the mechanism rather than the strategy: LoRA or QLoRA is how you train the small model on the curated trajectories, and it is also how you shrink a long house-style prompt into the weights at this volume. Watch the epoch count on a small dataset, and make sure the training data agrees with the prompt you will serve with.
why.dpo: Not needed: there is no preference data here and no complaint about tone or helpfulness. The ratings are correct-or-not labels, which is supervised signal rather than a comparison between two answers.
why.rlvr: Not needed: “what is the brokerage on an intraday equity trade” has no program-checkable answer in the sense this technique means - a verifier would just be the fee schedule, which is retrieval. Reinforcement on verifiable rewards is for maths, code, SQL and structured extraction.
why.ftagent: Not needed: this is a question-answering assistant, not a tool-using agent with proprietary schemas to learn. Nothing here describes tool calls being got wrong.

firstWhy.datacur: Correct that the logs need serious work before anything trains on them, and it is your second step. But curation serves a training objective, and the objective is in dispute - the vendor wants to train on fee schedules. Settle what goes in the weights and what goes in retrieval, then clean the data for that.
firstWhy.distill: The right answer to the cost question and the heart of the project. But distilling a model that has the fee schedule baked in means retraining after every SEBI circular, so the architecture decision has to be made first - otherwise you build the cheap model and inherit the expensive problem.
firstWhy.tuneeval: Right that the vendor's plan has no evaluation, and the baseline must be measured before anything is trained - start that immediately. As the sequence's first move, though, you would be measuring a baseline for a design nobody has agreed; decide what you are building, then decide what success looks like for it.

cases.model: Start with the prompt-versus-RAG-versus-fine-tune decision, because the vendor's proposal fails on it: brokerage and exchange fees change most months, and teaching facts that change monthly to the weights means a retrain per SEBI circular and a confidently stale model in between. Put the fee schedule in retrieval and reserve the weights for the skill - answering these forty intents in the house style - and build a strong prompt-and-RAG baseline so later gains are not overstated. Then curate the two lakh rated logs properly: deduplicate across training and evaluation rather than within training alone, strip customer names and PAN numbers before they enter weights no erasure request can reach, keep the agent ratings as labels, and rebalance so rare intents survive alongside order-status queries. Then distil into a small model, which is the right instrument for forty recurring intents at three million queries a month, using LoRA or QLoRA and watching the epoch count on a small dataset. Evaluate before and after, with a held-out set big enough to distinguish a real gain from noise and checks on the skills you did not target - and move traffic gradually after a head-to-head, not all at once as the vendor proposes. Preference tuning, verifiable rewards and trajectory tuning address problems this bot does not have.
cases.note: The whole case turns on one sentence about how often the fees change, and it sends the fee schedule to retrieval rather than to the weights. Case 2's agent must put its tool-calling skill in the weights because it cannot leave the premises, and Case 3's must put house style there - read what is volatile before deciding what to train.

decide: Read symptom 2 against symptom 4. Fees change most months after SEBI circulars, and the vendor wants to train a model on the fee schedules so it “knows the business”. What happens the month after training?

Before any training question, there is a prior one: which of the three places - the prompt, the retrieved context, or the weights - should each kind of knowledge live in? One of them is a bad home for anything that changes.
Prompt vs RAG vs Fine-Tune. The first pitfall - fine-tuning to teach facts that change monthly - is the vendor's proposal exactly, and the second tells you what to build before measuring anything.
datacur: Symptom 3: two lakh logged answers, each rated by an agent, and they are raw logs with duplicates, customer names and PAN numbers in them. What has to happen before any of that becomes training data?

Logs are not a dataset. Think about duplicates - and specifically about duplicates shared with your evaluation set - about personal data that cannot be removed from weights later, and about which intents dominate.
Training Data Curation and Synthetic Data. Read the pitfalls about training on raw logs and about deduplicating within the training data only.
distill: Symptom 1: forty recurring intents cover 80% of three million queries a month, and a frontier model already answers them well. What is the standard move for a narrow, high-volume task with a good teacher?
Have the small model learn to do what the big one already does on this slice. Note what symptom 4 proposes doing with the traffic afterwards, and why that is a named mistake.
Distillation into a Small Model. Read the pitfalls about unfiltered teacher mistakes and about switching all traffic before a head-to-head evaluation.
tuneeval: Look at the vendor's plan in symptom 4 and list what is missing from it. There is no measurement anywhere - not before, not after, not of anything the project was not aiming at.

Every tuning run needs a before and an after, on a set big enough to tell a real gain from noise, with nothing leaking between training and test - and it has to check what you did not set out to change.
Evaluate Before and After Tuning. All three pitfalls apply: leaked test items, a test set too small to separate a four-point gain from noise, and measuring only the target task.

drop.dpo: Preference tuning teaches which of two answers is better, from comparisons. What form are the two lakh labels in - comparisons, or correct-and-incorrect?
drop.rlvr: Verifiable rewards need an answer a program can check: maths, code, SQL, structured extraction. What would a verifier for “what is the brokerage on this trade” actually be - and where should that thing live?
drop.ftagent: Trajectory tuning teaches a small model to use your tools and schemas correctly. Which symptom here describes a tool call going wrong?

cases.firstHint: Your set is right. Before choosing a training technique, read symptom 2 once more and ask what it implies about anything you bake into weights - then ask which of your steps that decision changes.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: Forty intents at three million queries a month is the cost problem, and a small model is the answer to it.
Two lakh raw logs contain duplicates and PAN numbers, which must never reach the weights.
Fees change monthly, so what belongs in the weights and what belongs in retrieval has to be settled before anything is trained or curated.
whyFirst.why: Order from the decision the others inherit. Distillation is the right cost answer and the logs genuinely need cleaning - but curation serves a training objective, and distilling a model with the fee schedule baked in buys you a cheap model that needs retraining after every SEBI circular. Decide what is volatile and route it to retrieval, and both the dataset and the small model get designed correctly the first time.

cases.title: The agent that has to come in-house and keeps breaking its own tools
cases.brief: A public-sector bank runs an operations agent on a frontier model: it queries core banking, raises service requests, generates SQL for reconciliation and updates ticket records. Forty lakh tool calls a month. A new policy forbids sending this data off-premise, so the agent must move to a small open model on the bank's own GPUs. A first attempt has already been made and withdrawn.
evidence: Policy now forbids data leaving the premises, so a hosted frontier model is no longer an option for the forty lakh monthly tool calls.

The small open model gets the bank's proprietary tool schemas wrong about one call in five - wrong argument names, invented enum values. Ninety thousand successful agent trajectories from the frontier model are logged, alongside the failed and looping ones.
The withdrawn attempt trained on unfiltered logs. The model learned to loop, and because loss was computed over tool outputs too, it started inventing tool results that looked plausible.

The reconciliation step generates SQL, where correctness is checkable - the query runs and returns the right rows, or it does not - and hand-written training data for it is scarce. The only figure reported from the last attempt was that reward went up.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.ftagent: Start here, because the two failures of the withdrawn attempt are both specific to training on agent trajectories rather than general data problems. Learn the bank's proprietary schemas from successful runs only; mask the loss over tool outputs so the model never learns to generate tool results - that is why it began inventing them; and train in the same tool-call format you will serve in. Nothing in generic dataset hygiene would have told you to mask the loss.
why.datacur: Ninety thousand successful trajectories sitting beside the failed and looping ones is a dataset waiting to be built, not a dataset. Filter to successful runs, deduplicate across training and evaluation, strip customer data before it enters weights nothing can erase, and deliberately over-sample the rare tools - the ones used twice a week are where one-in-five schema errors hurt most, and they are exactly what frequency-weighted data drops.
why.rlvr: The SQL step is the textbook case: the answer is checkable by running the query, and hand-written training data is scarce while a verifier is cheap. Build the verifier on rows returned rather than on the query's shape, because rewarding format alone teaches the format and not the task - and the last attempt's only reported figure, that reward went up, is the exact pitfall of watching reward climb without checking held-out accuracy.
why.sft: Useful as the mechanism: LoRA or QLoRA on the filtered trajectories is how the schema knowledge gets in. Keep the epoch count modest and make sure the training format matches the serving format.
why.distill: Useful as the framing for the whole move - a small model learning what the frontier model already does well, with the added constraint that the data must stay on your infrastructure, which is one of this technique's stated reasons for existing. Run the head-to-head before moving traffic.
why.tuneeval: Useful and underdone: nobody measured the frontier model's tool-call accuracy before training, so there is no baseline to beat, and “reward went up” is not an evaluation. Measure before, hold out properly, and check the tools you did not target.
why.decide: Useful, and here the decision is already made for you by policy rather than by preference - which is worth noticing, because it is the one circumstance where fine-tuning is not optional. The schema knowledge is also genuinely stable, unlike Case 1's fee schedule, so the weights are the right home for it.
why.dpo: Not needed: there are no preference pairs and no complaint about tone or helpfulness. A tool call is right or wrong, which is supervised or verifiable signal rather than a comparison.

firstWhy.datacur: Very close, and the two overlap - filtering to successful runs is both. But the thing that broke the last attempt worst was computing loss over tool outputs, which taught the model to invent results, and no amount of general dataset cleaning would have caught that. It is a property of how you train on trajectories.
firstWhy.rlvr: A genuinely good fit for the SQL step and the most interesting technique here. But it improves one step, while one call in five across all tools is wrong - and a verifier that rewards queries whose format looks right would teach exactly the wrong thing if the schema knowledge is not there first.
firstWhy.decide: Worth stating, and the answer is unusually clean: policy forbids the hosted model, so fine-tuning is not a choice. That makes it a sentence in the plan rather than a first step - the decision is already made, and the question is how to execute it.

cases.model: Start with fine-tuning for tool use and agent trajectories, because the withdrawn attempt failed in two ways that only this technique warns about: it trained on unfiltered logs, so the model learned to loop, and it computed loss over tool outputs, so the model learned to invent tool results. Train on successful trajectories only, mask the loss over tool outputs, and train in the same tool-call format you will serve in. Then curate properly - filter to successful runs, deduplicate across training and evaluation, strip customer data before it reaches weights nothing can erase, and over-sample the rarely used tools, because frequency-weighted data drops exactly the schemas the model gets wrong. Then apply verifiable rewards to the reconciliation SQL, where the query either returns the right rows or does not and hand-written data is scarce: build the verifier on returned rows rather than query shape, since rewarding format teaches format, and report held-out accuracy rather than that reward went up. Use LoRA or QLoRA as the mechanism, frame the whole move as distillation under a data-residency constraint, and establish the frontier model's tool-call accuracy as the baseline you must beat. Preference tuning has no role: a tool call is right or wrong.
cases.note: This is the one case in the module where fine-tuning was not a choice - policy removed the alternative - and the failures were all in how, not whether. Two of them, looping runs and invented tool results, are invisible unless you know that trajectory training has its own rules.

ftagent: Read symptoms 2 and 3 together: proprietary tool schemas wrong one call in five, ninety thousand successful trajectories logged next to the failed and looping ones, and a withdrawn attempt whose model learned to loop and to invent tool results. What kind of training is this, and what two mistakes were made?
Training on what an agent did, step by step, rather than on question-and-answer pairs. One mistake was which runs went in; the other was which tokens the loss was computed over.

Fine-Tuning for Tool Use and Agent Trajectories. All three pitfalls are in symptom 3 and the one before it: unfiltered logs teaching failed runs, loss on tool outputs teaching invented results, and a format mismatch between training and serving.
datacur: Symptom 2 again, from the data side: ninety thousand successful trajectories, and the failed and looping ones sitting in the same place. Plus a question nobody has asked - which tools appear how often?

Build the dataset deliberately: what to include, what to deduplicate against, what personal data must never reach the weights, and which rare cases need over-sampling because the natural frequencies would bury them.
Training Data Curation and Synthetic Data. Read the pitfalls about raw logs and about a task where a few intents dominate while rare ones matter most.
rlvr: Symptom 4: the reconciliation step generates SQL, which either runs and returns the right rows or does not, hand-written training data is scarce, and the only number anyone reported was that reward went up. What technique is being described - and how was it misreported?
When you cannot write many examples but you can cheaply check an answer, the checker becomes the training signal. Be careful what the checker actually rewards, and what you report afterwards.
Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards. All three pitfalls are here: rewarding format alone, weak tests wrong answers pass, and watching reward climb without held-out accuracy.

drop.dpo: Preference tuning learns from pairs where one response is better than another. Is a tool call with an invented enum value worse than another call, or simply wrong?

cases.firstHint: Your three are right. Now ask what actually broke the last attempt: one of its two failures - a model that began inventing tool results - comes from a training detail that only one technique on this page talks about.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: The last attempt trained on unfiltered logs containing failed and looping runs, which is a data problem.
Training on trajectories has rules of its own - which runs to include, and masking the loss over tool outputs - and breaking the second is why the model invented tool results.
The SQL step has a cheap verifier and scarce training data, which is the highest-leverage place to train.
whyFirst.why: Order by what explains the actual failure. Filtering the logs is necessary and the SQL verifier is the most elegant opportunity here - but the withdrawn model started fabricating tool results, and no amount of dataset hygiene would have prevented that. It happened because loss was computed over the tool outputs, which is a rule specific to training on agent trajectories, and it decides how the dataset is built.

cases.title: The letter writer reviewers rewrite every time
cases.brief: An insurer drafts claim rejection letters with a model and has reviewers approve them before they go out. Volume is modest - a few hundred letters a day - and cost is not the issue. The issue is that reviewers rewrite most of what they are given, and a previous tuning attempt made things stranger rather than better.
evidence: Reviewers rewrite 70% of drafts, almost always for tone - too blunt or too hedged. They say it is far easier to pick the better of two drafts than to write down the rule, and 60,000 such comparisons already exist in the review tool.
A previous supervised run trained on 4,000 approved letters for twelve epochs. The model now reproduces whole paragraphs verbatim, including one real case reference, and there was no held-out set.
The house format is fixed - headings, clause citations, the mandatory ombudsman paragraph - and the model gets it wrong in about one letter in eight.
Only the target task was measured. Nobody checked whether the tuned model still handles the Hindi and Marathi letters it used to write competently.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.sft: Start here, even though it is not the biggest symptom, because the standard sequence is supervised tuning then preference tuning - and a fixed house format with a mandatory paragraph is exactly what supervised tuning is for. Redo it properly: the previous run's problem was method, not technique - twelve epochs on 4,000 examples is how a model memorises, and reproducing a real case reference verbatim is overfitting with a privacy incident attached. Fewer epochs, a held-out set, and training data that agrees with the production prompt.
why.dpo: This is the bigger symptom and the right instrument for it: 70% of drafts rewritten for tone, with reviewers saying comparison is far easier than articulating the rule, and 60,000 comparisons already collected. That is preference tuning's exact brief. Mind the three traps: inconsistent preferences cancel out, so check reviewer agreement; if approved drafts are systematically longer you will teach verbosity rather than tact; and too low a beta lets the model drift away from skills it already has.
why.tuneeval: Nobody has checked what the last run broke, and the question in symptom 4 is the important one: a model tuned on English rejection letters may well have lost the Hindi and Marathi competence it had. Measure the baseline, hold out a set large enough to separate a real gain from noise, keep test letters out of training, and explicitly test the skills you are not targeting.
why.datacur: Useful, and symptom 2 shows why: a real case reference now lives in the weights because the training set was raw approved letters. Strip identifiers and claim references, deduplicate against the evaluation set, and balance the rejection reasons so the common one does not define the house voice.
why.decide: Useful to state: tone and house format are stable, which is what makes weights the right home - the opposite of Case 1, where the facts changed monthly. Also build the prompt baseline, because a well-written style prompt may close more of the format gap than anyone has tested.
why.rlvr: Not needed, though it is a tempting half-fit: the format could be checked by a validator, and a validator is worth having as an output guardrail. But rewarding format alone is this technique's named pitfall - you would get perfectly structured letters with the tone problem intact, which is 70% of the complaint.
why.distill: Not needed: a few hundred letters a day is low volume and the brief says cost is not the issue. Distillation answers a bill, and there is no bill here.
why.ftagent: Not needed: writing a letter involves no tool calls and no schemas.

firstWhy.dpo: The largest symptom by far - 70% rewritten for tone - and the data is already sitting in the review tool, so going first feels obvious. But preference tuning refines a model's choices on top of what it can already produce, and this one gets the mandatory ombudsman paragraph wrong in one letter of eight. You would be teaching good taste to a letter that is still malformed, and the conventional sequence is supervised tuning first for a reason.
firstWhy.tuneeval: Right that nobody knows what the last run broke, and the Hindi and Marathi question needs answering before anything else ships - start measuring immediately. As the sequence's first move, though, evaluation brackets the training rather than replacing it, and you already know the previous attempt overfitted.
firstWhy.datacur: Correct and urgent in one respect: a real case reference is in the weights, which is a privacy problem as much as an overfitting one. But that happened because of how the training was run - twelve epochs on 4,000 examples - as much as because of what went in, so fix the method and the data together.

cases.model: Start by redoing supervised fine-tuning properly, because the fixed house format - headings, clause citations, the mandatory ombudsman paragraph, wrong in one letter of eight - is what supervised tuning is for, and because preference tuning conventionally comes after it. The previous run's faults were method: twelve epochs on 4,000 examples is how a model memorises, and a verbatim real case reference is overfitting plus a privacy incident, so use fewer epochs, a held-out set, stripped identifiers, and training data consistent with the production prompt. Then apply preference tuning to the tone problem, which is 70% of the complaint and already has 60,000 reviewer comparisons behind it - checking inter-reviewer agreement so noisy preferences do not cancel out, watching for chosen drafts being systematically longer and thereby teaching verbosity, and keeping beta high enough that the model does not drift off its general skills. Evaluate before and after throughout, on a held-out set large enough to tell a four-point gain from noise, with no leakage, and explicitly test the Hindi and Marathi letters nobody has checked. State the prompt-versus-weights decision too: tone and format are stable, so weights are the right home, but measure a strong style prompt first. Verifiable rewards would teach format while leaving the tone untouched, and there is no cost problem to distil for and no tool to learn.
cases.note: The biggest symptom is not always the first move: tone is 70% of the complaint and still waits behind a format the model gets wrong one time in eight, because preference tuning refines what a model can already produce. Across the three cases the first move came from the structure of the problem - what is volatile, how the data was trained on, what order the techniques stack in.

sft: Symptom 3: a fixed house format - headings, clause citations, a mandatory ombudsman paragraph - wrong in one letter in eight. Symptom 2: a previous run on 4,000 letters for twelve epochs now reproduces whole paragraphs verbatim. Same technique, one use and one abuse.

Teaching a consistent format and house style from examples is the core job here. The previous attempt's failure is one of this technique's named pitfalls, and it is about a number nobody should have set that high.
Supervised Fine-Tuning with LoRA and QLoRA. Read the pitfalls about too many epochs on small data and about having no held-out set - both are symptom 2.
dpo: Symptom 1: 70% of drafts rewritten for tone, reviewers saying it is far easier to pick the better of two drafts than to write the rule, and 60,000 such comparisons already in the review tool. What kind of signal is that, and what trains on it?

Comparisons, not demonstrations. There is a technique for behaviour that is easier to compare than to write down - and three ways it goes wrong, one of which involves the length of the preferred answers.
Preference Tuning with DPO. Read all three pitfalls: inconsistent preferences cancelling out, chosen answers being systematically longer and teaching verbosity, and beta so low the model drifts.
tuneeval: Symptom 4: only the target task was measured, and nobody checked whether the tuned model still writes competent Hindi and Marathi letters. What question has gone unasked about every run so far?
Not just whether the thing you aimed at improved, but what else moved - and whether your test set is clean and large enough for the answer to mean anything.
Evaluate Before and After Tuning. The third pitfall - measuring only the target task and missing lost skills - is symptom 4 exactly.

drop.rlvr: Verifiable rewards train on answers a program can check. A letter's format could be validated - but what does this technique's first pitfall say happens if you reward format alone, and what fraction of the complaint is about tone?
drop.distill: Distillation puts a narrow, high-volume task on a small model to cut cost or latency. What does the brief say the volume is, and what does it say about cost?
drop.ftagent: Trajectory tuning teaches a model to use your tools correctly. How many tool calls does writing a letter involve?

cases.firstHint: Your three are right, and the biggest number is not the first move. Ask what preference tuning operates on: it refines choices between things the model can already produce - and read symptom 3 again.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: 70% of drafts are rewritten for tone and 60,000 comparisons already exist, so the data and the symptom both point one way.
A real case reference is now baked into the weights, which is a privacy problem that cannot be undone by a later run.
The model still gets the mandatory format wrong one letter in eight, and preference tuning only refines what the model can already produce.
whyFirst.why: Order by how the techniques stack. Tone is the larger complaint and the comparison data is ready; the memorised case reference is a real problem that must be fixed as part of the retraining. But preference tuning adjusts choices between outputs a model can already generate, and a letter missing its mandatory ombudsman paragraph is not yet a valid output - teach the format first, then the taste.

decide.t: Answering with RAG on a large model costs ₹0.55 a query. A fine-tuned small model costs ₹0.10 a query plus ₹60,000 a month for training refreshes, evaluation and hosting. Above what monthly volume is the tuned model cheaper?
decide.a: Set 0.55v = 0.10v + 60,000, so 0.45v = 60,000 and v ≈ 133,333 queries a month. Below that, the fixed cost of tuning is not recovered, before counting the engineering time to keep it current.
iv: When would you fine-tune rather than use RAG?

When the gap is behaviour rather than knowledge: a consistent format, tone or narrow skill, or a shorter prompt at high volume, and you have enough good examples. Facts, especially ones that change, belong in retrieval, where they can be updated and cited. The two combine well: a tuned model that reads retrieved context.
Why not fine-tune a model on your documents so it knows them?

Fine-tuning is poor at adding new facts reliably, the facts go stale as documents change, and the model cannot cite a source. Research has found that tuning on unfamiliar facts can even raise hallucination. Retrieval updates instantly and shows where each answer came from.
mis: Tuning on facts that change every month
Put them in retrieval and cite sources
Comparing a tuned model with a weak prompt
Beat the best prompted and RAG baseline first

sft.t: LoRA adds two matrices A (r × d) and B (d × r) beside a frozen d × d weight. For d = 4,096 and rank r = 16, how many trainable parameters does one such weight get?
sft.a: 2 × 4,096 × 16 = 131,072, against 16,777,216 in the frozen matrix: about 0.78%. Across the model, adapters usually total well under 1% of the parameters, which is why they train and store cheaply.
iv: How do LoRA and QLoRA differ?

Both freeze the base model and train small low-rank adapters. QLoRA also stores the frozen base in 4-bit NF4, which cuts memory by roughly four times compared with 16-bit weights, so a 70B model can be tuned on a single 48–80 GB GPU. Quality is usually close to LoRA; training is somewhat slower.
How do you know an SFT run has overfitted?

Training loss keeps falling while loss or accuracy on a held-out set stops improving or gets worse, often after too many epochs on a small dataset. Outputs start copying training examples verbatim. Hold out a test set from the start, evaluate every epoch and keep the best checkpoint.
mis: Training three or more epochs on 500 examples
Use more data or fewer epochs, and watch held-out loss
Computing loss on the user’s turns too
Train only on the assistant’s replies

dpo.t: You have 5,000 preference pairs, and 30% of them are labelled the wrong way round. If each wrong pair cancels one correct pair, how many pairs of net useful signal remain?
dpo.a: Correct pairs: 3,500; wrong: 1,500. Net 3,500 − 1,500 = 2,000, which is 5,000 × (1 − 2 × 0.3). Cleaning labels to 5% noise would give 4,500: more than double the signal from the same collection effort.
iv: How does DPO differ from RLHF with PPO?

RLHF trains a separate reward model on preferences and then optimises the policy against it with reinforcement learning. DPO skips both: it uses a closed-form loss on chosen and rejected pairs that raises the likelihood of the chosen answer relative to a frozen reference model. It is simpler, more stable and cheaper, though online methods can still do better on some tasks.
What does beta control in DPO?

How far the tuned model may drift from the reference. A small beta lets it move a lot, which can win preferences but hurt other skills; a large beta keeps it close, so it learns less. Values around 0.1 are a common starting point.
mis: Preferring the longer answer in most pairs
Balance lengths, or the model learns to be verbose
Running DPO on a raw base model
Start from an SFT model that already follows instructions

rlvr.t: In GRPO, eight answers are sampled for one prompt and two are correct (reward 1, others 0). Using the group mean as the baseline, what is the advantage of a correct answer?
rlvr.a: Mean reward = 2/8 = 0.25, so a correct answer’s advantage is 1 − 0.25 = 0.75 and a wrong one’s is −0.25 (before dividing by the group standard deviation, 0.43, which gives about 1.73 and −0.58). If all eight were right or all wrong, every advantage would be zero and the prompt would teach nothing.
iv: What makes a reward verifiable, and why does it matter?

A program can decide it: an answer matches the key, code passes tests, a query returns the right rows. No learned reward model is needed, so there is less to game. But a weak verifier can still be exploited, for example by rewarding format or by tests that miss cases, so the checker itself needs review.
What is reward hacking and how do you spot it?

The model finds a way to raise the reward without doing the task: matching a format, gaming weak tests, or exploiting a bug in the checker. You spot it when training reward keeps rising but accuracy on a held-out set, checked independently, does not. Inspect samples and strengthen the verifier.
mis: Rewarding format or length
Reward only verified correctness, with format as a small bonus at most
Trusting training reward as the score
Track held-out accuracy with an independent check

distill.t: A frontier model answers 3 million queries a month at ₹0.90 each. A distilled student costs ₹0.08 a query and takes 80% of traffic; the rest stays on the frontier model. What share of the monthly bill is saved, in percent? (Ignore training cost.)
iv: Why filter the teacher’s outputs before distilling?

The student learns whatever it is shown, including the teacher’s mistakes. Keeping only answers that pass an automatic checker, a judge or a sample review raises the student’s quality and stops it copying errors. Including the teacher’s rationales can also help a small student learn how, not just what.
How would you deploy a distilled model safely?

Route traffic to it gradually, starting with the easy, common intents, and keep the teacher as a fallback for low-confidence or unusual queries. Compare the student with the teacher on held-out and live samples, and check the provider’s terms on training with its outputs.
mis: Distilling unfiltered logs
Filter out wrong answers first
Switching all traffic at once
Route gradually with the teacher as fallback

tuneeval.t: Two models are compared on n = 200 test cases each, with accuracy near 80%. Using 1.96 × √(2 × 0.8 × 0.2 ÷ n), what is the 95% margin of error on the difference, in accuracy points?
tuneeval.a: √(2 × 0.16 ÷ 200) = √0.0016 = 0.04, times 1.96 = 0.0784, or about 7.8 points. A 4-point gain is within the noise; with 1,000 cases the margin is 3.5 points. (Scoring both models on the same items, a paired test, tightens this.)
iv: How can a fine-tuning gain be overstated?

Test cases that leaked into training (contamination), a test set too small to separate the models, comparing with the untuned base instead of the best prompted baseline, or cherry-picking the checkpoint on the test set. Deduplicate, use a large held-out set, compare with a strong baseline and report confidence intervals.
What should you check besides the target task?

What tuning may have broken: general knowledge and reasoning, instruction following, safety refusals and other tasks the model handles. Tuning on a narrow task can cause forgetting elsewhere, so run general and safety regression suites on the base and tuned models with the same settings.
mis: A 50-case test set
Use hundreds or thousands of cases and report intervals
Only testing the target task
Add general and safety regression suites

datacur.t: Udaan Lend has 50,000 logged loan queries. Deduplication removes 18% of them, decontamination then removes 400 rows that match the eval set, and the EMI-date intent, 30% of what remains, is cut to one row in three. Finally 5,000 verified synthetic rows are added. How many rows is the final training set?
datacur.a: 50,000 × 0.82 = 41,000 after deduplication; 41,000 − 400 = 40,600. The EMI-date intent is 0.3 × 40,600 = 12,180 rows; keeping one in three leaves 4,060, so 8,120 go and 32,480 remain. Adding 5,000 synthetic rows gives 37,480, fewer than the 50,000 raw rows but a better model.
iv: How would you build a fine-tuning dataset from production logs?

Pull logs and expert-written examples into one label set and one format. Deduplicate exactly and with MinHash for near-copies, and remove anything that overlaps the eval set. Rank likely label errors with a tool like cleanlab and have people review the hardest ones. Scrub personal data, rebalance dominant intents and languages, and fill thin intents with synthetic rows from a stronger model that are filtered and spot-checked. Version the dataset and measure every change on a clean held-out set.
When is synthetic data a good idea, and what can go wrong?

It helps when real examples of an intent, language or edge case are scarce, or cannot be used for privacy reasons. It goes wrong when rows are used unchecked: the generator’s factual errors, a narrow style that differs from real users, and copies of eval items all pass into training, and repeated rounds of training on generated data can narrow what a model produces. Generate from a stronger model, verify with an independent classifier, rules and a human sample, deduplicate against real and eval data, and keep real data as the backbone.
mis: Deduplicating the training data but never checking it against the eval set
Run the same near-duplicate check between training rows and eval items, and drop the overlaps from training
Adding generated rows straight from the model
Filter with independent checks and a human spot-check, and track how many are rejected

ftagent.t: A task costs ₹6 with the large model and ₹0.40 with the tuned 8B. At 50,000 tasks a month, what is the monthly saving in ₹?
ftagent.a: (6 − 0.40) × 50,000 = 5.6 × 50,000 = ₹2,80,000 a month. The ₹42,000 data and training cost pays back in under a week.
iv: How would you fine-tune a small model to run an agent?

Collect trajectories from logs or a teacher in a sandbox, keep only runs whose end state was verified, format them in the serving chat and tool template, train LoRA with loss on assistant turns only, and evaluate end-to-end task success on held-out tasks.
Why mask tool outputs during training?
If tool outputs carry loss, the model learns to write them, and at run time it may invent a result instead of calling the tool.
mis: Training on all logs
Keep verified successful trajectories only
Scoring by text similarity
Score end-to-end task success in a sandbox

gloss: fine-tuning
Continuing to train a pretrained model on your own examples so its weights change.
SFT
Supervised fine-tuning: training on example inputs paired with the desired outputs.
LoRA
Low-rank adaptation: freezing the model and training small added matrices instead of all the weights.
QLoRA
LoRA on a base model stored in 4-bit precision, so large models fit in less GPU memory.
adapter
The small set of trained weights added by LoRA; it can be saved, swapped or merged into the model.
rank (r)
The size of a LoRA adapter’s inner dimension; higher ranks can learn more and cost more.
overfitting
Learning the training examples so closely that performance on new cases gets worse.
DPO
Direct preference optimisation: training on chosen and rejected answer pairs without a separate reward model.
beta (DPO)
How strongly the tuned model is kept close to the reference model during preference tuning.
RLVR
Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards: rewards that a program can check, such as a matching answer.
GRPO
Group relative policy optimisation: sample several answers per prompt and favour those that score above the group average.
reward hacking
Raising the reward by exploiting the reward’s weaknesses rather than doing the task.
distillation
Training a smaller student model on the outputs of a larger teacher model.
contamination
Test cases, or near-copies of them, appearing in the training data, which inflates scores.
near-duplicate
Two texts that are almost the same, such as a template with a different name or amount, usually found by comparing overlapping character or word n-grams.
MinHash
A compact signature that estimates the Jaccard similarity of two texts; with locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) it finds near-duplicates without comparing every pair.
confident learning
A method that uses a model’s out-of-sample predicted probabilities to estimate which examples are probably mislabelled, so people review those first.
synthetic data
Training examples generated by a model rather than collected from real use; useful for gaps, and only safe after filtering and verification.
trajectory
The full sequence of an agent run: user turns, tool calls, tool results and replies.
assistant-only loss
Training loss computed only on assistant turns, with user and tool turns masked.
teacher model
A stronger model whose outputs are used to create training data for a smaller one.

distill.name: Model Routing and Tiering
distill.note: A distilled student is only useful behind a router: easy, common queries go to the student and hard or low-confidence ones to the teacher.

distill.name: Training Data Curation and Synthetic Data
distill.note: Distillation builds training data from a teacher’s outputs; the same filtering and verification apply to synthetic rows for rare intents.

distill.name: Serving Engines and Continuous Batching
distill.note: A distilled small model is usually self-hosted on one of these engines.

distill.name: Fine-Tuning for Tool Use and Agent Trajectories
distill.note: Teacher trajectories distil a large model's agent behaviour into a small one.

tuneeval.name: System-Level Eval
tuneeval.note: Before-and-after evaluation of a tuned model is a system-level eval on a clean held-out set, plus regression suites.

tuneeval.name: Canary Releases and Prompt Flags
tuneeval.note: Offline evals decide whether a tuned model may ship; a canary on a slice of live traffic confirms it before full rollout.

tuneeval.name: EU AI Act Risk Tiers
tuneeval.note: High-risk systems need documented accuracy and robustness; before-and-after evaluation of tuned models supplies it.

tuneeval.name: Training Data Curation and Synthetic Data
tuneeval.note: Decontaminating the training set against the eval set is what keeps the before-and-after comparison honest.

tuneeval.name: Speech in Indian Languages
tuneeval.note: Fine-tuning a recogniser on 8 kHz calls needs the same before-and-after discipline: per-language WER on a held-out set, checking no language got worse.

tuneeval.name: Quantisation for Inference (FP8, INT4, KV Cache)
tuneeval.note: Quantisation changes a model, so run the same before-and-after evals as for fine-tuning.

decide.name: RAG Grounding Metrics
decide.note: If the gap is knowledge rather than behaviour, fix retrieval and measure it with RAG evals before considering tuning.

decide.name: JSON Schema and Constrained Decoding
decide.note: Many format problems that seem to need fine-tuning are solved by strict structured outputs at no training cost.

rlvr.name: Reasoning Models and Thinking Budgets
rlvr.note: Reasoning models are largely trained with reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards such as maths answers and passing tests.

sft.name: Few-Shot Examples
sft.note: Few-shot examples teach in the prompt on every call; fine-tuning bakes the same examples into the weights once, which pays off at high volume.

sft.name: Training Data Curation and Synthetic Data
sft.note: SFT learns exactly what the dataset shows; curation decides what that is: deduplicated, correctly labelled, balanced and free of personal data.

sft.name: Fine-Tuning for Tool Use and Agent Trajectories
sft.note: Agent fine-tuning uses the same LoRA machinery, with trajectories and assistant-only loss.

dpo.name: LLM-as-a-Judge
dpo.note: An LLM judge can label preference pairs at scale, but its biases, such as preferring longer answers, pass straight into DPO.

datacur.name: Supervised Fine-Tuning with LoRA and QLoRA
datacur.note: SFT learns exactly what the dataset shows; curation decides what that is: deduplicated, correctly labelled, balanced and free of personal data.

datacur.name: Evaluate Before and After Tuning
datacur.note: Decontaminating the training set against the eval set is what keeps the before-and-after comparison honest.

datacur.name: Distillation into a Small Model
datacur.note: Distillation builds training data from a teacher’s outputs; the same filtering and verification apply to synthetic rows for rare intents.

datacur.name: PII Detection and Redaction
datacur.note: PII detection and redaction, applied to logs before they become training rows, keeps Aadhaar, PAN and phone numbers out of the model’s weights.

datacur.name: User Feedback Loops and the Data Flywheel
datacur.note: Consented, redacted feedback examples become curated fine-tuning or preference data.

ftagent.name: Supervised Fine-Tuning with LoRA and QLoRA
ftagent.note: Agent fine-tuning uses the same LoRA machinery, with trajectories and assistant-only loss.

ftagent.name: Distillation into a Small Model
ftagent.note: Teacher trajectories distil a large model's agent behaviour into a small one.

ftagent.name: Process-Level Eval
ftagent.note: Step-level process evals check the tuned model's tool calls, not just the final answer.

gifs.datacur: Animated scene for Training Data Curation and Synthetic Data. First, the raw training logs of a fictional NBFC, 50,000 loan queries, are broken down in bars: 9,000 near-copies, 4,500 wrong labels, 6,000 rows holding personal data and 15,000 rows in the single EMI-date intent, and a red badge warns that 400 rows are near-copies of eval items. Next, the dataset shrinks step by step: 41,000 rows after deduplication, 40,600 after decontamination against the eval set, 32,480 after rebalancing the EMI-date intent, then 37,480 after adding verified synthetic rows, with a badge noting that labels were fixed, personal data was scrubbed and 5,000 of 8,000 generated rows were kept. Finally, held-out results compare raw and curated data: on the raw data the full eval set reported 84.9% but the honest score was 81.4%, while the curated set scores 90.6% honestly; rare-intent accuracy rises from 58% to 87%, and a green badge reads "37,480 clean rows beat 50,000 raw".
gifs.decide: On 500 policy questions a prompt scores 71%, retrieval 93% and fine-tuning 76%; when the wordings change the tuned model drops further, so rules go in the prompt, changing facts in retrieval and behaviour in fine-tuning.
gifs.distill: A teacher at 92% and ₹0.90 a query produces 50,000 answers, filtered to 44,000, which train an 8B student scoring 91% at ₹0.08; routing 80% of traffic to the student and hard cases to the teacher cuts the bill by about 70%.
gifs.dpo: Advisers pick the better of two answers; a first DPO run wins 61% of comparisons but answers grow 45% longer, and after balancing lengths it wins 64% with answers 8% shorter and a one-point general drop.
gifs.ftagent: A booking trajectory is shown turn by turn: the user asks for 2 seats from Delhi to Jaipur on Friday, the assistant calls search_trains, the tool returns 3 trains, the assistant calls hold_seat, the tool returns a PNR, and the assistant confirms. Assistant turns are marked loss and user and tool turns are masked. 2,000 of 3,100 runs verified in the sandbox train a LoRA adapter on an 8B model, and task success rises from 48 to 73 percent, against 78 percent for the teacher.
gifs.rlvr: Eight sampled answers, two correct, give a group mean of 0.25 so right answers get +0.75; a reward for format reaches 95% while accuracy stays at 42%, but rewarding only matching answers lifts accuracy to 66% in step with the reward.
gifs.sft: A frozen 8B weight matrix with two thin LoRA matrices beside it trains about 0.5% of the parameters; training memory falls from 130 GB for full fine-tuning to 19 GB with LoRA and 7 GB with a 4-bit QLoRA base, and format compliance rises from 81% to 97%.
gifs.tuneeval: A claimed 12-point gain on 50 test cases, 30% of them leaked from training, shrinks to 4 ± 3.5 points on 1,000 clean cases, and regression suites show general knowledge down 6 and safety refusals down 3.

header.lede: Changing a model’s weights is powerful, costly and often unnecessary. Decide first whether the prompt or the context should change instead; when tuning is right, adapt cheaply with LoRA, teach preferences, reward what a program can check, distil a large model into a small one, and prove the result before it ships.
